title: Cocaine likely factor in death
subtitle: TV thief was pinned on sidewalk, inquest hears
article: The inquest jury came up with only one recommendation after hearing that continued cocaine use likely played a significant role in the death of James Kiteley.

It recommended the government ministry overseeing police in this province explore the "cost feasibility" of equipping all police vehicles with portable defibrillators and that patrol officers be trained in using "this potential life-saving tool."

However, the coroner's inquest heard earlier Tuesday from forensic pathologist Dr. John Fernandes that without the cocaine use that probably caused Kiteley's hardened arteries and enlarged heart, the 36-year-old should have lived through a fight he had with two men over the theft of their TV.

Acquaintances Jurgen Porkristl and son Leif pinned Kiteley and held him face-down on the sidewalk near their Brighton Street home until police arrived, after they caught him walking down the street with their TV on Feb. 13, 2011.
"If you subtract heart disease and cocaine ... I would have expected him to survive in that short a time (that he was restrained)," Fernandes said.

The inquest heard Monday Porkristl's friend called 911 immediately after the duo pinned Kiteley down and police arrived in three minutes. An ambulance was called within a minute after Constable Ken Breitenbach handcuffed Kiteley, then turned him onto his back and discovered him lifeless.

Kiteley's heart disease likely resulted from cocaine use, Fernandes said. "In a 36-year-old, that amount of heart disease is unusual ... he had significant hardening of the arteries for someone his age."
He said the added stress of the fight and being pinned down forced Kiteley's heart to work harder and increased his vulnerability.
The other major contributing factors were being face-down on the sidewalk with two people piled on top, and being put in a headlock by the theft victim's son, Fernandes said.

Coroner's counsel David King had no suggested recommendations for the jury to consider. "This is a case of a series of unfortunate events that culminated in Mr. Kiteley's death," he said. "A man has lost his life, but sometimes bad things just happen. Saying (that) nothing could have been done differently ... doesn't mean we don't value Mr. Kiteley's life."

King did suggest the jury rule the death an accident, which it did. Although the Porkristls may have contributed to Kiteley's death, King said they had no foresight, thought or intention that he would die. They also called police right away, and Porkristl was within his rights as a property owner to hold Kiteley for police, King added.

Once Kiteley was taken to hospital, he was found to have cocaine, marijuana and narcotics in his system, Fernandes said. Cocaine has a direct effect on the heart and in an altercation, if a person is compromised by bad artery disease, cocaine "worsens the situation and the heart can't tolerate this further challenge."
Fernandes, asked by Coroner Dr. Jack Stanborough if he had any advice for the jury's recommendations, had little to suggest, "other than the obvious - don't use cocaine."

However, he added that people with heart disease should get it managed, and "if I were to encounter a large person involved in an altercation, I'd try to quiet that down as soon as possible and use minimum amounts of interventions."
Fernandes described Kiteley as slightly obese, but also muscular and likely about 220 pounds.
Fernandes suggested the jury change his originally stated cause of death to "the combined effects of restraint asphyxia, heart disease and cocaine use," which the jury later adopted in its verdict.
Fernandes's original cause was "restraint asphyxia due to compression of the torso and external neck compression."
Stanborough extended his condolences to Kiteley's family and said although the inquest doesn't give closure, he hoped it brought some peace.
The family declined to comment to The Spectator.
